title: Text ordering vs phone ordering for restaurants
seoTitle: Text ordering vs phone ordering for restaurants | ROAL
description: Compare text ordering with phone ordering, including speed, labor, order accuracy, costs, and what works best for busy owners.
question: Should my restaurant use text ordering or phone ordering?
answer: Text ordering can work for simple reorders, but phone ordering is usually better when guests need menu help, modifiers, substitutions, or fast answers about hours and pickup. A phone host can take the order, confirm it back, collect the caller’s name and phone, and send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen without asking staff to stop what they’re doing.
summary: Compare the two order channels and pick the one that fits your menu, staff load, and peak-hour call volume.
intro:
Text ordering sounds easy because the guest can type without waiting on hold. Phone ordering is often better for real restaurant orders because people ask about sold-out items, sizes, toppings, substitutions, parking, and ready times.

For most independent restaurants, the real question is not “text or phone?” It is which one turns more calls into clean tickets without adding extra work for the counter or kitchen. That is where an AI phone host like ROAL can help, because it answers calls, takes pickup and delivery orders from the live menu, and sends the ticket straight to the kitchen screen.

sections.h2: What is the real difference between text ordering and phone ordering?
sections.body:
Text ordering usually means the guest sends a message, taps choices, and waits for a reply or a link. Phone ordering means the guest says the order out loud, asks follow-up questions, and gets an immediate response.

For a restaurant, the difference shows up in the details. On a phone call, the host can hear things like “extra crispy,” “no onions,” “gluten-free crust,” or “half fries, half salad.” That matters for pizza shops, delis, and takeout spots where modifiers change the order.

Here is a simple way to think about it:

| Channel | Best for | Common weak spot |
|---|---|---|
| Text ordering | Simple repeats and scheduled orders | Guests may still need help with menu questions |
| Phone ordering | Custom orders, questions, and quick clarifications | Needs someone or something to answer the line |

A useful script for either channel is: “What size would you like, and any toppings or notes?” The difference is whether a guest must type that out or can say it in one shot.

sections.h2: When does text to order restaurant setup make sense?
sections.body:
A text to order restaurant flow can work well when your menu is short, your regulars already know what they want, and the order is mostly the same every time. It is also useful for guests who do not want to talk, especially during a busy lunch rush.

But text ordering gets shaky when the guest needs live help. If someone asks, “Do you still have meatballs?” or “Can I swap fries for salad?” you need a fast way to answer. If the system is too rigid, the guest may abandon the order or call anyway.

Use this quick checklist before leaning on text ordering:

- Your menu is simple enough to click through without confusion.
- Your most common orders do not need many special notes.
- Someone is available to answer text questions quickly.
- You do not mind sending the guest back and forth to confirm details.

Worked example: say a $28 average order, and 20 text orders come in on a busy night. If even 5 of those need staff back-and-forth, that is time pulled from the counter or kitchen. Plug in your own order size and volume to see whether text saves time or just moves the work around.

sections.h2: When is phone ordering the better fit?
sections.body:
Phone ordering is usually the better fit when your menu has lots of modifiers, substitutions, or item names customers do not always remember. It is also better when callers want immediate answers about hours, address, parking, or the menu.

That is why many restaurants prefer a phone host over a text-only flow. The caller can say, “Two chicken parms, one with no cheese, and one Caesar salad with dressing on the side,” and the host can repeat it back before sending the ticket. ROAL does this from the restaurant’s live menu and does not offer items marked sold out.

A practical call script looks like this:

“Thanks for calling. Is this for pickup or delivery?”

Then:

1. Take the items and modifiers.
2. Ask for the caller’s name and phone.
3. Give a ready time.
4. Read the order back.
5. Send the ticket to the kitchen screen.

That flow is hard to beat during a rush, because the guest gets answers now and staff do not have to decode a text thread later.

sections.h2: How do the costs compare for a busy restaurant?
sections.body:
Cost is where the difference becomes very clear. Third-party delivery apps commonly take roughly 15-30% commission per order. Human answering services usually bill per minute or per call. Many AI phone tools charge a fixed monthly fee per location, often around $79 to $599, whether orders come in or not.

ROAL uses a different model: $0.90 per completed phone order, with no monthly fee, no setup fee, no per-minute fee, and no contract. Calls, questions, and test calls are free. That makes the math easier when traffic changes from week to week.

Here is a simple swap-in example:

| Example | Math | Result |
|---|---:|---:|
| 120 completed orders in a month | 120 × $0.90 | $108 |
| 300 completed orders in a month | 300 × $0.90 | $270 |
| 50 completed orders in a month | 50 × $0.90 | $45 |

Now compare that with a fixed monthly plan in the rough $79 to $599 range, or with commission on each order through delivery apps. Plug in your own monthly order count and average ticket, then compare the total cost of each channel against the labor time it saves.

sections.h2: Which one creates fewer mistakes at the counter and in the kitchen?
sections.body:
The best channel is the one that turns the caller’s request into a clean ticket with the fewest handoffs. Text can reduce mishearing, but it can also create confusion when the guest abbreviates items, leaves out details, or sends a string of short messages.

Phone ordering reduces that problem by letting the host confirm the order in one conversation. ROAL takes items, sizes, modifiers, and notes; collects the caller’s name and phone; quotes a ready time; and confirms the order back before sending it to the kitchen screen.

A short quality checklist for owners:

- The order should show item names the kitchen knows.
- Modifiers should be written clearly, not buried in chat.
- The caller’s name and phone should be captured once.
- Sold-out items should be blocked from the order.
- Allergy-sensitive questions and manager requests should go to staff with a summary.

Example: if a caller says “large pepperoni, half mushrooms, no onions,” the kitchen should see that same order cleanly. If your current text flow makes staff retype half the message, you are not saving labor.

sections.h2: How do I set up phone ordering without losing my main number?
sections.body:
You do not need to give up your restaurant’s current line. With ROAL, the owner pastes the restaurant website, Google Maps link, or “Name, City” at /try, and ROAL builds a phone host in about two minutes from public menu and business info. The owner can test-call it in the browser before going live, with no sign-up needed.

When you are ready, the owner claims the host and ROAL gives each location its own phone line automatically. Then you forward the restaurant’s existing number to it, either for all calls or only when busy or unanswered. The restaurant keeps its own number, and forwarding can be turned off any time.

A simple rollout plan:

1. Check that your menu, hours, and address are current.
2. Build the host from your site or menu files.
3. Test a few common orders and questions.
4. Claim the host and forward calls.
5. Watch the live tickets and call history in the dashboard.

For forwarding setup, confirm the exact code with your carrier or phone system and test with a real call. If you want a starting point, use [call forwarding codes by carrier](/tools/call-forwarding-codes) and double-check your plan.

sections.h2: What should I choose if I want the simplest path for my staff?
sections.body:
If your staff already juggle the counter, kitchen, and pickups, the simplest path is usually the one that removes the most interruptions. For many restaurants, that means phone ordering handled by an AI phone host instead of asking a cashier to stop ringing up walk-ins.

ROAL also helps with the questions that do not fit a simple order: hours, address, parking, menu items, reservations, catering, complaints, and manager requests. Questions it cannot answer land in an inbox, and after you answer once, it knows it from then on.

Use this final decision rule:

- Choose text ordering if your orders are mostly repeats and your guests prefer messaging.
- Choose phone ordering if your menu needs conversation and your callers ask questions first.
- Choose ROAL if you want phone ordering, kitchen tickets, and menu answers without adding a fixed monthly bill.

If you want to see whether it fits your shop, [build a free test host](/try) from your website or menu and call it before you decide.

takeaways: Text ordering works best for simple, repeat orders; phone ordering works better for custom restaurant orders.
A phone host can confirm modifiers, collect caller details, and send a clean kitchen ticket.
ROAL charges per completed phone order, not a monthly fee, which makes cost easier to match to volume.
You can keep your existing restaurant number and forward calls only when you want to.

faq.q: Is text ordering better than phone ordering for a restaurant?
faq.a: It depends on your menu and your guests. Text ordering is fine for simple repeat orders, but phone ordering is usually better when callers need help with modifiers, sold-out items, hours, or ready times. For many independent restaurants, phone ordering creates fewer back-and-forth messages and cleaner tickets.

faq.q: Can I keep my restaurant’s current number if I switch to phone ordering?
faq.a: Yes. With ROAL, the restaurant keeps its own number and forwards calls to the host when needed. You can forward all calls or only unanswered and busy calls, and you can turn forwarding off any time.

faq.q: Does an AI phone host take payment cards over the phone?
faq.a: No. ROAL does not take card numbers over the phone. Payment happens at pickup or however the restaurant already takes payment. That keeps the call focused on the order and the ready time.

faq.q: What kinds of calls should go to staff instead of text or phone ordering?
faq.a: Tricky calls should go to staff, including catering requests, complaints, allergy-sensitive questions, and manager requests. ROAL passes those along with a summary so the team can handle them directly.
